evidence_set: 17 healthy adults (9 men, 8 women; mean age 27.3) who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days (mean 398 days, median 365, range 30 to 1,825 since last use) each completed six 8.5-hour sessions at least a week apart: flower with 0, 10 or 25 mg THC loaded, smoked in a small handheld pipe or vaporized in a Volcano Medic vaporizer and inhaled from a balloon, over 10 minutes. Method order was counterbalanced across people and dose order randomized within each method.

Flower from the US National Institute on Drug Abuse supply with 13.4% delta-9-THC (placebo batch under 0.01%); the same weight of plant material (186.6 mg) in every session, with placebo material mixed in to reach 10 mg. The 'dose' is the THC in the material loaded; the paper does not report how much THC left each device.

Drug-effect rating (0 to 100), mean (SD) peak change: smoked 45.7 (26.4) at 10 mg and 66.4 (28.6) at 25 mg; vaporized 69.5 (26.4) and 77.5 (23.4); placebo (0 mg) sessions 11.2 (15.9) smoked and 2.1 (5.2) vaporized. Vaporized exceeded smoked at 10 mg (flagged P below .05) and no difference was flagged at 25 mg. Editors' calculation (unpaired, conservative): vaporized minus smoked 23.8 points (95% CI 5.4 to 42.2) at 10 mg and 11.1 (-7.2 to 29.4) at 25 mg.

Peak whole-blood THC, mean (SD) ng/mL: vaporized 7.5 (5.5) at 10 mg and 14.4 (9.4) at 25 mg; smoked 3.8 (5.9) and 10.2 (12.4). Peak at the first sample (10 minutes), back to zero within 4 hours in every condition. The paper reports no test or interval for the difference between methods. Editors' calculation (unpaired): vaporized minus smoked 3.7 ng/mL (-0.3 to 7.7) at 10 mg and 4.2 (-3.5 to 11.9) at 25 mg.

Heart rate, mean (SD) peak rise in beats per minute: smoked 11.3 (10.4) at 10 mg and 19.1 (17.1) at 25 mg; vaporized 23.3 (11.8) and 26.8 (16.6); placebo (0 mg) sessions -3.7 smoked and -4.3 vaporized. Only the 10 mg difference between methods was flagged (P below .05); editors' calculation (unpaired), vaporized minus smoked: 12.0 beats per minute (4.2 to 19.8) at 10 mg and 7.7 (-4.1 to 19.5) at 25 mg. Peak at the first measurement (10 minutes); back to baseline within 3 hours.

Task performance, peak change from baseline. Digit Symbol Substitution (number correct): vaporized -8.3 at 10 mg and -13.8 at 25 mg, both below the vaporized placebo session; smoked +3.4 and -7.0, neither different from its placebo session. Differences between methods at the 10 and 25 mg doses were flagged for three contrasts only: Divided Attention distance at 10 mg, and Digit Symbol Substitution attempted and correct at 25 mg (the Table also carries the between-method flag on two 0 mg vaporized cells, Divided Attention distance and Divided Attention total correct). Deficits typically peaked 30 to 60 minutes after dosing and in some instances had not returned to baseline at 6 to 8 hours.

Adverse events as reported: two people vomited (one after 25 mg vaporized, one after 25 mg smoked) and one had hallucinations after 25 mg vaporized. No counts are given for placebo or 10 mg sessions and no other events are listed; the paper gives no incidence figures behind the abstract's statement of increased incidence of adverse effects at 25 mg, and these three are the only events it lists.

Limits stated by the authors: a limited range of doses, one type of cannabis (raw plant material, high THC, low cannabidiol), one vaporizer at a fixed temperature, enrolment limited to people who rarely use cannabis, and a sample too small to study individual characteristics. They note that the largest amount given (0.19 g of 13.4% THC flower) is smaller and weaker than prerolls sold in dispensaries (about 1 g, often over 18% THC, citing a 2018 paper that was not read here).

evidence_set: 2,553 young adults (mean age 19.3; 57.9% women; 1,188 Hispanic, 47.3% of the 2,510 with race and ethnicity data) from a Southern California school-based cohort answered one survey between June 2018 and October 2019, a year after high-school graduation (75% participation). Outcome data were available for 2,194 (bronchitic symptoms), 2,396 (wheeze) and 2,389 (shortness of breath). Bronchitic symptoms were daily cough for 3 months in a row, congestion or phlegm other than with a cold, and/or bronchitis in the previous 12 months; wheeze in the previous 12 months; shortness of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill.

Shortness of breath and cannabis vaping: sociodemographic model raised at 3 or more days (1.67, 1.09 to 2.53) and for past 6 months but not past 30 days (1.35, 1.04 to 1.75); in the full model no level was reliably raised (0.90, 0.57 to 1.40; 1.25, 0.86 to 1.84; 1.55, 0.81 to 2.96; 3 or more days 1.41, 0.80 to 2.48).

Editors' reading of Table 3: odds of bronchitic symptoms were raised even in people whose last cannabis vaping was more than 6 months before the survey (1.73, 1.01 to 2.96), against 2.19 to 2.79 for vaping on days in the past 30, so the data show no clear gradient with recency; this argues for caution about an effect of recent vaping and for residual confounding. The Methods describe no product, device, source, additive or amount of cannabis vaping, and no record of tobacco in joints or blunts (the questionnaire is in the eAppendix, which was not read).

Weekly hospital admissions for the national vaping lung injury outbreak (EVALI) peaked at 215 in the week of 15 September 2019, within the period (June 2018 to October 2019) in which this survey was taken; the survey asked about nicotine and about THC or hash oil/dabs vaping but not about specific products or additives, and its Methods describe no question on whether anyone had that injury.

evidence_set: CDC case definitions as printed in the paper: confirmed and probable cases both need vaping or dabbing in the 90 days before symptom onset, a lung infiltrate on chest imaging and no evidence in the medical record of an alternative plausible diagnosis; confirmed cases also need a negative respiratory viral panel, a negative influenza test (if local epidemiology supports influenza testing) and negative results for all other clinically indicated infection tests; probable cases may have an infection identified, or incomplete testing, when the clinical team judges the infection is not the sole cause of the lung injury. State and local health departments assigned case status.

Weekly hospital admissions for EVALI reported to CDC (Figure 1: 2,398 patients by week of admission, February 2019 to 14 January 2020) peaked at 215 in the week of 15 September 2019 and declined steadily after that to the end of the data.

Limits given by the authors: product-use data missing for 24% of patients and many not interviewed; the emergency visit query may have been affected by awareness of the outbreak; coverage of the surveillance system uneven and changing over time. The case counts are of hospitalized patients (the Methods say states report hospitalized or deceased patients); the report does not report deaths or what happened to patients after discharge (it says long-term consequences need long-term follow-up).

Second-hand context quoted by the authors from CDC and FDA web pages and earlier CDC reports (none read here): more than 2,400 hospitalized patients and 52 deaths as of 12 December 2019 (CDC web page); 78% under 35; nearly half (47%) needed intensive care for respiratory failure (earlier CDC report). FDA testing (FDA web page) found vitamin E acetate in 49% of case-associated THC product samples and none of 197 case-associated nicotine products; in Minnesota (earlier MMWR report) 0 of 10 products seized in 2018 contained it against 20 of 20 THC products seized in September 2019.
